results.prompt: Build a loan calculator with a slider for the amount.
results.raw:
Here's an interactive calculator — drag the sliders and every figure updates instantly.

:::intelligent-ui{v="1"}
root = Stack([sAmount, btnRow, sRate, sYears, grid1, ch1])
sAmount = Slider("Loan amount", $amount, 10000, 1000000, 5000)
btnRow = Row([b1, b2, b3, b4])
b1 = Button("150k", @Set($amount, 150000))
b2 = Button("300k", @Set($amount, 300000))
b3 = Button("500k", @Set($amount, 500000))
b4 = Button("Reset", @Reset($amount))
sRate = Slider("Interest rate (% per year)", $rate, 1, 15, 0.25)
sYears = Slider("Term (years)", $years, 1, 30, 1)
grid1 = Grid([m1, m2, m3])
m1 = Metric("Monthly payment", monthly, "Principal + interest", "positive")
m2 = Metric("Total interest", interest, "Cost of borrowing", "warning")
m3 = Metric("Total paid", total, "Over the full term")
ch1 = Chart("pie", "Where the money goes", ["Principal", "Interest"], [{name: "Split", values: [$amount, interest]}])
$amount = 250000
$rate = 5.5
$years = 25
x = $rate * $years / 100
x2 = x * x
x4 = x2 * x2
x6 = x2 * x4
n = $years * 12
factor = 1 + x / 2 + x2 / 12 - x4 / 720 + x6 / 30240
monthly = $amount / n * factor
total = monthly * n
interest = total - $amount
:::

**How to read it:** the monthly figure is a standard amortised payment (equal instalments over the term). Notice how interest is highly sensitive to the term — stretching a loan from 15 to 30 years shrinks the monthly payment but can nearly double the total interest paid. Figures are indicative and exclude fees, insurance and taxes.

Here's an interactive mortgage calculator — drag the sliders and the payment, totals and payoff curve update instantly (native calculation, no round-trip).

:::intelligent-ui{v="1"}
root = Stack([secLoan, m1, g1, ch1])
secLoan = Section("Your loan", [sp, sd, sr, sy])
sp = Slider("Home price", $price, 500000, 10000000, 50000)
sd = Slider("Down payment", $down, 0, 2000000, 25000)
sr = Slider("Interest rate (%)", $rate, 0.5, 15, 0.1)
sy = Slider("Term (years)", $years, 5, 30, 1)
m1 = Metric("Monthly payment", payment, "Principal and interest", "positive")
g1 = Grid([m2, m3, m4])
m2 = Metric("Loan amount", loan, "Price minus down payment")
m3 = Metric("Total interest", ti, "Over the full term", "warning")
m4 = Metric("Total paid", tc, "Principal plus interest")
ch1 = Chart("area", "Remaining balance", labels, series)
$price = 3000000
$down = 600000
$rate = 4.5
$years = 25
loan = $price - $down
mr = $rate / 1200
n = $years * 12
payment = loan * mr / (1 - 1 / ((1 + mr) ** n))
ti = payment * n - loan
tc = payment * n
labels = ["Now", "5 years", "10 years", "15 years", "20 years", "25 years", "30 years"]
b0 = loan
b5 = loan * (1 + mr) ** 5 - payment * ((1 + mr) ** 5 - 1) / mr
b10 = loan * (1 + mr) ** 10 - payment * ((1 + mr) ** 10 - 1) / mr
b15 = loan * (1 + mr) ** 15 - payment * ((1 + mr) ** 15 - 1) / mr
b20 = loan * (1 + mr) ** 20 - payment * ((1 + mr) ** 20 - 1) / mr
b25 = loan * (1 + mr) ** 25 - payment * ((1 + mr) ** 25 - 1) / mr
b30 = loan * (1 + mr) ** 30 - payment * ((1 + mr) ** 30 - 1) / mr
v0 = b0
v5 = b5 > 0 ? b5 : 0
v10 = b10 > 0 ? b10 : 0
v15 = b15 > 0 ? b15 : 0
v20 = b20 > 0 ? b20 : 0
v25 = b25 > 0 ? b25 : 0
v30 = b30 > 0 ? b30 : 0
series = [{name:"Balance", values:[v0, v5, v10, v15, v20, v25, v30]}]
:::

A few things worth knowing: the monthly figure covers principal + interest only — property tax, insurance and fees come on top. Two levers move it most: every extra year of term lowers the payment but raises total interest sharply, while a larger down payment cuts both the payment and the interest bill without stretching the term. If you tell me your currency and whether you want taxes/fees included, I can extend it.

BMI is just weight (kg) divided by height squared (m²). Adjust the sliders and the number, category and scale update instantly.

:::intelligent-ui{v="1"}
root = Stack([card1, card2, card3])
card1 = Card("Your measurements", [sH, sW, row1])
sH = Slider("Height (cm)", $height, 120, 220)
sW = Slider("Weight (kg)", $weight, 30, 200)
row1 = Row([bH, bW])
bH = Button("Reset height", @Reset($height))
bW = Button("Reset weight", @Reset($weight))
card2 = Card("Your result", [m1, badge1, prog1])
m1 = Metric("BMI", bmiRounded, "kg/m²", tone)
badge1 = Badge(category, tone)
prog1 = Progress("Position on the 15–40 scale", pos, category)
card3 = Card("Reference", [tbl1])
tbl1 = Table("WHO classification", ["BMI range", "Category"], [["Below 18.5", "Underweight"], ["18.5 – 24.9", "Normal weight"], ["25.0 – 29.9", "Overweight"], ["30.0 and above", "Obese"]])
$height = 175
$weight = 75
bmi = $weight / (($height / 100) * ($height / 100))
bmi10 = bmi * 10
bmiRounded = (bmi10 - bmi10 % 1) / 10
category = bmiRounded < 18.5 ? "Underweight" : bmiRounded < 25 ? "Normal weight" : bmiRounded < 30 ? "Overweight" : "Obese"
tone = bmiRounded < 18.5 ? "warning" : bmiRounded < 25 ? "positive" : bmiRounded < 30 ? "warning" : "negative"
pos = bmiRounded < 15 ? 0 : bmiRounded > 40 ? 100 : (bmiRounded - 15) * 4
:::

BMI is only a rough screening number — it doesn't distinguish muscle from fat, so athletes and very muscular people can read "overweight" while carrying little fat, and it says nothing about where weight sits on the body. For a fuller picture, pair it with waist circumference and body-fat percentage.

results.prompt: Build a savings calculator with a monthly deposit slider.
results.raw:
Here's a calculator you can play with — drag the deposit slider and everything updates instantly.

:::intelligent-ui{v="1"}
root = Stack([metrics, controls, chartCard])
$monthly = 500
$initial = 5000
$rate = 6
metrics = Grid([m1, m2, m3])
m1 = Metric("Balance in 10 years", bal10, "Annual compounding", "positive")
m2 = Metric("Total deposited", deposited, "Starting balance + deposits")
m3 = Metric("Interest earned", interest, "Growth on top of deposits", "positive")
controls = Section("Assumptions", [slMonthly, slStart, slRate, quick])
slMonthly = Slider("Monthly deposit", $monthly, 0, 5000, 100)
slStart = Slider("Starting balance", $initial, 0, 50000, 500)
slRate = Slider("Expected annual return (%)", $rate, 0, 12, 0.5)
quick = Row([btn250, btn500, btn1000, btnReset])
btn250 = Button("$250 / month", @Set($monthly, 250))
btn500 = Button("$500 / month", @Set($monthly, 500))
btn1000 = Button("$1000 / month", @Set($monthly, 1000))
btnReset = Button("Reset", @Reset($monthly))
chartCard = Card("Projected balance by year", [ch1])
ch1 = Chart("area", "", ["Year 1","Year 2","Year 3","Year 4","Year 5","Year 6","Year 7","Year 8","Year 9","Year 10"], [{name:"Balance", values:[bal1, bal2, bal3, bal4, bal5, bal6, bal7, bal8, bal9, bal10]}])
g = 1 + $rate / 100
dep = $monthly * 12
bal1 = $initial * g + dep
bal2 = bal1 * g + dep
bal3 = bal2 * g + dep
bal4 = bal3 * g + dep
bal5 = bal4 * g + dep
bal6 = bal5 * g + dep
bal7 = bal6 * g + dep
bal8 = bal7 * g + dep
bal9 = bal8 * g + dep
bal10 = bal9 * g + dep
deposited = $initial + dep * 10
interest = bal10 - deposited
:::

Two things to keep in mind: the projection assumes deposits are credited once a year with annual compounding, not monthly, so it's a mild understatement of the true monthly-compounded result. And the return rate is an assumption, not a guarantee — try moving it down to 3% to see how much of the ending balance comes from contributions rather than growth.

Here's a three-mode percentage calculator — drag the sliders and the results update instantly.

:::intelligent-ui{v="1"}
$pct = 15
$base = 250
$part = 60
$whole = 300
$from = 200
$to = 250

root = Tabs([tab1, tab2, tab3])

tab1 = Tab("X% of Y", [s1a, s1b, m1, b1])
s1a = Slider("Percentage (%)", $pct, 0, 100, 1)
s1b = Slider("Value", $base, 0, 1000, 10)
m1 = Metric("Result", v1, "X% of the value")
v1 = $pct / 100 * $base
b1 = Button("Reset all", @Reset($pct))

tab2 = Tab("X is what % of Y", [s2a, s2b, m2, b2])
s2a = Slider("Part", $part, 0, 500, 1)
s2b = Slider("Whole", $whole, 1, 500, 1)
m2 = Metric("Result", v2, "Part as a share of whole")
v2 = $part / $whole * 100
b2 = Button("Reset all", @Reset($part))

tab3 = Tab("Percent change", [s3a, s3b, m3, b3])
s3a = Slider("From", $from, 0, 1000, 1)
s3b = Slider("To", $to, 0, 1000, 1)
m3 = Metric("Change", v3, "Increase or decrease between the two values", $to >= $from ? "positive" : "negative")
v3 = ($to - $from) / $from * 100
b3 = Button("Reset all", @Reset($from))
:::

- **X% of Y** multiplies: percent ÷ 100 × value.
- **X is what % of Y** divides: part ÷ whole × 100.
- **Percent change** compares: (to − from) ÷ from × 100 — a negative result means a decrease.

Tell me if you'd rather type exact numbers instead of dragging sliders, or want a fourth mode such as "add/remove X%".

Here's an interactive converter — pick a tab, drag the amount, and choose your units.

:::intelligent-ui{v="1"}

$lenVal = 10
$lenA = "m"
$lenB = "cm"

$wB = "g"

lenBF = $lenB == "mm" ? 0.001 : $lenB == "cm" ? 0.01 : $lenB == "m" ? 1 : $lenB == "km" ? 1000 : $lenB == "in" ? 0.0254 : $lenB == "ft" ? 0.3048 : 1609.344
lenResult = $lenVal * lenAF / lenBF
tabWt = Tab("Weight", [wSlider, wSelects, wMetric, wDiv, wTable])

wSelB = Select("To", $wB, ["mg","g","kg","t","oz","lb"])
wMetric = Metric("Result", wResult)
wDiv = Divider()
wTable = Table("Quick reference", ["From", "To"], [["1 kg","2.2046 lb"],["1 oz","28.35 g"],["1 t","1000 kg"],["1 lb","0.4536 kg"]])
wAF = $wA == "mg" ? 0.000001 : $wA == "g" ? 0.001 : $wA == "kg" ? 1 : $wA == "t" ? 1000 : $wA == "oz" ? 0.0283495 : 0.453592
wBF = $wB == "mg" ? 0.000001 : $wB == "g" ? 0.001 : $wB == "kg" ? 1 : $wB == "t" ? 1000 : $wB == "oz" ? 0.0283495 : 0.453592
wResult = $wVal * wAF / wBF
tabTemp = Tab("Temperature", [tSlider, tSelects, tMetric, tDiv, tTable])
tSlider = Slider("Amount", $tVal, -50, 300, 1)
tSelects = Row([tSelA, tSelB])
tSelA = Select("From", $tA, ["C","F","K"])
tSelB = Select("To", $tB, ["C","F","K"])
tMetric = Metric("Result", tResult)
tDiv = Divider()
tTable = Table("Quick reference", ["From", "To"], [["0 °C","32 °F"],["100 °C","212 °F"],["0 K","-273.15 °C"],["-40 °C","-40 °F"]])
tC = $tA == "C" ? $tVal : $tA == "F" ? ($tVal - 32) * 5 / 9 : $tVal - 273.15

Everything recalculates instantly as you move the slider or change a unit — no round trip needed. Length and weight convert via a base unit (metres, kilograms), while temperature uses the proper offset formulas, so Fahrenheit and Kelvin offsets come out correct. If you'd like more categories (volume, area, speed, data sizes) or a two-field layout where you can also type the source value, say the word.

**What it means**

- **The trend is up, and it's accelerating.** Growth is not linear: the first half adds roughly $30k of monthly revenue, the second half adds nearly $60k. Compounding, not a one-off spike.
- **There's a genuine soft patch in April and July.** Both dips are followed by a recovery that exceeds the prior peak, which is the signature of a healthy business (seasonality or a demand pause) rather than a plateau or decline.
- **Momentum is intact right now.** The last three months are the three highest, and December is +8% over November — the recent direction matters more than the yearly average.
- **The risk is extrapolation.** A 65% quarterly pace rarely persists; if you plan headcount or spend against it, model the trend flattening rather than continuing to compound.

Show the costs and explain the largest one.
results.raw:
I don't have your actual cost data in this conversation, so the figures below are an illustrative annual breakdown (typical for a small team) — send me the real numbers and I'll rebuild it with your values.

:::intelligent-ui{v="1"}
$headcount = 10
root = Stack([g1, ch1, t1, d1, s1, m2])
g1 = Grid([m1, m3])
m1 = Metric("Total cost", "935 000 kr", "Illustrative annual run rate")
m3 = Metric("Largest item", "Salaries · 620 000 kr", "About two-thirds of total", "warning")
ch1 = Chart("bar", "Cost by category (kr)", ["Salaries","Cloud & hosting","Software licenses","Marketing","Office & admin"], [{name:"Cost", values:[620000,145000,78000,52000,40000]}])
t1 = Table("Breakdown", ["Category","Amount (kr)","Share of total"], [["Salaries","620 000","66%"],["Cloud & hosting","145 000","16%"],["Software licenses","78 000","8%"],["Marketing","52 000","6%"],["Office & admin","40 000","4%"]])
d1 = Divider()
s1 = Slider("Headcount", $headcount, 4, 20)
m2 = Metric("Total at this headcount", total, "62 000 kr per person + 315 000 kr fixed")
total = $headcount * 62000 + 315000
:::

**The largest cost is salaries — and it dominates the picture.**

- **Why it's biggest:** it's the only line that scales directly with people. Add a person and you add salary, employer contributions, benefits, laptop, and usually a license seat — roughly 62 000 kr/year each in this example. The other categories are either fixed (office, base hosting) or discretionary (marketing, tools).
- **Why it matters more than its size:** at ~66% of total, salaries set the sensitivity of everything else. A 10% change there moves the whole cost base by about 6.6%; the same 10% cut on cloud hosting moves it by only 1.6%.
- **Why it's hard to trim fast:** salaries are recurring and contractual (notice periods, commitments), whereas licenses and marketing can usually be paused within a month.
- **Levers, in order of impact:** headcount plan and backfill discipline → contractor vs. permanent mix → automation of manual work → renegotiating the second-largest line (cloud/hosting), which is small in absolute terms but the fastest to change.
- **Watch-out:** if one line is above ~60% of the total, you have concentration risk — model the budget against a hiring freeze and against two extra hires, and see which one breaks it.

Use the slider above to see how the total responds: every additional person adds 62 000 kr and 315 000 kr stays fixed. If you paste your actual categories and amounts, I'll replace the illustrative numbers, rank them exactly, and pinpoint the sensitivity of your real largest item.

results.prompt: Compare React vs Vue vs Svelte.
Which is better for a startup, Stripe or Adyen?
results.raw:
For the vast majority of startups the answer is **Stripe** — Adyen only starts to win once you have serious, predictable volume and a reason to care about the last few basis points.

:::intelligent-ui{v="1"}
root = Stack([cmp1, d1])
cmp1 = Comparison("Stripe vs Adyen for a startup", [{name:"Stripe",attributes:["Self-serve signup — live in hours","2.9% + 30¢ per online card payment","Interchange++ available on custom/volume deals","Huge docs, SDKs, plugins, ecosystem","Best-in-class subscriptions, invoicing, tax","No contract, no minimum volume","Support is email/chat, thin at scale"]},{name:"Adyen",attributes:["Sales-led onboarding — days to weeks","Interchange++ pricing — cheaper at scale","One platform for online + in-store/POS","Local acquiring in many countries","Requires volume commitment & contract","Enterprise support, strong fraud/risk tooling","250+ local payment methods built in"]}])
d1 = Divider()
:::

**Why Stripe wins early:** you can integrate today with no contract, no minimums, no sales call, and you get billing, subscriptions, Checkout, Radar, and Tax as add-ons the moment you need them. For a company that doesn't yet know its volume or its market, flexibility is worth far more than a slightly better rate.

**When Adyen is the better call:**
- You're processing roughly €10M+ a year and interchange++ pricing saves you real money.
- You sell in-store as well as online and want one provider and one reconciliation.
- You're expanding across many countries and want local acquiring to lift authorization rates.
- You have a payments/ops person who can manage the relationship and integration work.

**The pragmatic path:** start on Stripe, keep your payment layer thin (a gateway abstraction, or something like Spreedly/Stripe-only first), and revisit Adyen once your volume makes the negotiation worth it. Switching later is a project, not a disaster — but switching *prematurely* costs you weeks you don't have.

One caveat: if you're in a market Stripe doesn't serve well (or you need a specific local method as your primary rail), evaluate regionally — Adyen, Mollie, Buckaroo, or a local PSP may beat both.
